lead: A level gives a height difference from two staff readings: backsight minus foresight. Differential, fly and profile levelling are three ways to repeat that one piece of arithmetic. Differential levelling chains many setups to reach a far or high point. Fly levelling is a quick link between two benchmarks, or a run to bring the level to the work. Profile levelling takes closely spaced points along a line, and cross-sections across it, for a road or canal. The arithmetic never changes; only the spacing of points and the purpose change.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for RL, benchmark and height of instrument, and Chapter 3.2 for a level in adjustment.

sections.h3: Differential levelling: a chain of setups

blocks.text: Differential levelling finds the RL of a point that is too far, too high or too low for one instrument setup. The level is set up once, a backsight is read on a point of known RL, and the height of instrument is fixed. A foresight on the next point then gives that point's RL. When the next point is out of sight, or the line of sight is too long, the last point becomes a change point (CP). The staff is read as a foresight, the instrument moves, and the same staff is read as a backsight from the new setup. A run with one setup is simple levelling. A run with change points is compound levelling. Differential levelling is the general method that uses as many setups as needed.
HI = RL<sub>BM</sub> + BS; RL<sub>new</sub> = HI − FS
blocks.where: HI is the height of instrument in m; RL<sub>BM</sub> is the reduced level of the backsight point in m; BS is the backsight staff reading in m; RL<sub>new</sub> is the reduced level of the foresight point in m; FS is the foresight staff reading in m.

blocks.text: The field arithmetic is checked at the end: the sum of backsights minus the sum of foresights must equal the last RL minus the first RL. The standard booking layout is in Chapter 3.4.

blocks.where: ΣBS is the sum of all backsights in m; ΣFS is the sum of all foresights in m; RL<sub>last</sub> is the reduced level of the final point in m; RL<sub>first</sub> is the reduced level of the starting benchmark in m.

sections.h3: Fly levelling and the closing check

blocks.text: Fly levelling is a fast run between two points, usually two benchmarks. It uses only backsights and foresights; it takes no intermediate sights. Its purpose is to carry the level to the work, or to make a quick height link. Some syllabi call it loose levelling or connecting levelling. A fly run gives a height difference. It does not give a check unless it starts and ends on the same benchmark, or ends on a second benchmark of known RL.

Check levelling is a run that returns to the benchmark it started from. The closing error is the measured RL of that benchmark minus its known RL. If the closing error is within the permissible limit, the run is accepted. The limit is set by the survey specification, often as a multiple of √K, where K is the run length in km. A large error means the run must be repeated.

Profile levelling maps the ground along a line. For a road, canal or railway, the line is the centre line. Points are fixed at equal chainages, such as 0, 20, 40 m. A backsight is taken on the benchmark, then an intermediate sight (IS) at each chainage. When the instrument moves, the last staff point becomes a change point: it is read as a foresight and then as a backsight. The reduced levels are plotted with chainage on the horizontal axis and RL on the vertical axis. This is the longitudinal section.

At selected chainages, cross-sections are taken at right angles to the centre line, with staff readings left and right up to the width of the work. Cross-sections give the shape across the road or canal and are used for earthwork, drainage and setting out. Contour maps use the same RL idea, as Chapter 3.6 shows.

sections.h3: Field rules for all three patterns

items: Keep sights short; a long sight increases reading error and the corrections for curvature and refraction (Chapter 3.5).
Keep backsight and foresight lengths roughly equal so instrument error cancels (Chapter 3.2).
Hold the staff vertical; a leaning staff reads too large.
The staff at a change point must not move between the foresight and the next backsight. If it moves, the chain is broken and the RLs after that point are wrong.
Read the staff without parallax, and book every reading before leaving the setup.

blocks.text: These rules matter more than the arithmetic, because the arithmetic cannot repair a bad reading.

figure.caption: The same height-of-instrument arithmetic feeds all three patterns; the difference is how the points are spaced and what the run is for.

spec.title: Which levelling pattern
spec.aria: A flowchart splitting a levelling run into differential, fly and profile levelling, with all three feeding into one booking and reduction step.

examples.question: A benchmark B has RL 50.000 m. A level is set up between B and a change point C. The backsight on B is 1.500 m and the foresight on C is 2.000 m. The instrument is moved and set up beyond C. The backsight on C is 1.200 m and the foresight on Q is 1.700 m. Find the RL of Q and apply the arithmetic check.
steps: RL of change point C = HI − FS = 51.500 − 2.000 = 49.500 m.
Setup 2: new HI = RL<sub>C</sub> + BS = 49.500 + 1.200 = 50.700 m.
Last RL − first RL = 49.000 − 50.000 = −1.000 m. The arithmetic check agrees.
examples.answer: The RL of Q is 49.000 m, which is 1.000 m below benchmark B; the arithmetic check agrees with ΣBS − ΣFS = −1.000 m.
examples.check:
bs1 = 1.500
fs1 = 2.000
bs2 = 1.200
fs2 = 1.700
rl_bm = 50.000
hi1 = rl_bm + bs1
rl_cp = hi1 - fs1
hi2 = rl_cp + bs2
rl_q = hi2 - fs2
sum_bs = bs1 + bs2
sum_fs = fs1 + fs2
arith = sum_bs - sum_fs
last_first = rl_q - rl_bm
for v in [hi1, rl_cp, hi2, rl_q, arith, last_first]:
    print(f'{v:.3f}')

traps: A fly levelling run that ends on a different benchmark is not a check. Only a run that returns to its starting benchmark, or ends on a second benchmark of known RL, gives a closing error.
Forgetting that a change point is read twice: once as a foresight before the instrument moves, and once as a backsight after. If the staff moves, the height chain is broken.
Treating an intermediate sight as a change point. An IS gives the RL of one point only; it does not carry the height forward to the next setup.
Reversing the arithmetic check. ΣBS − ΣFS equals last RL − first RL, not first RL − last RL.
Calling the height of instrument the ground RL. HI is the height of the line of sight; the ground RL is HI minus the staff reading.

quiz.a: It is levelling that finds the RL of a point by using one or more instrument setups, with backsights and foresights, and change points when the instrument must move.

quiz.q: What two readings are taken at a change point?
quiz.a: A foresight from the old setup and a backsight from the new setup, on the same staff held at the same point.

quiz.q: Why does a fly levelling run give a height difference but not always a check?
quiz.a: A fly run only links two points. It measures their height difference. A check needs a known RL at the end, or a return to the starting benchmark, so the measured RL can be compared with the known RL.

quiz.q: State the difference between a longitudinal section and a cross-section in profile levelling.
quiz.a: A longitudinal section is the ground profile along the centre line at fixed chainages. A cross-section is the ground profile at right angles to the centre line at one chainage, taken left and right up to the width of the work.

quiz.q: A benchmark has RL 100.000 m. The backsight on it is 1.250 m and the foresight on a point P is 2.100 m. Find the RL of P.
A run starts at RL 25.000 m. ΣBS = 4.200 m and ΣFS = 5.100 m. Find the final RL and test the arithmetic check.
quiz.a: ΣBS − ΣFS = 4.200 − 5.100 = −0.900 m. Final RL = 25.000 − 0.900 = 24.100 m. Last RL − first RL = 24.100 − 25.000 = −0.900 m, so the check agrees.

quiz.q: In a profile run, an intermediate sight is taken at chainage 40 m. The instrument must move before chainage 60 m. What must be done at chainage 40 m, and why?
quiz.a: The staff at chainage 40 m must be treated as a change point: read it as a foresight, move the instrument, then read the same staff as a backsight. An intermediate sight alone cannot carry the height forward, because the new HI must be computed from a known RL after the move.

beyond: Not for the exam. Digital levels record staff readings electronically and can reduce a profile run as the staff is read, which reduces booking mistakes. Total stations and GNSS now carry height control over long routes, but the level still sets the local bench mark because it is more precise over short sights. Laser scanners and drones produce dense ground profiles for earthwork checks. Search for digital levelling, level run misclosure, and machine control for graders and excavators.
